subtitle: Journal-club style ICU update: PICO, key results, appraisal, bedside impact, and medical English.

script.heading: Intro
sentences: Welcome to Critical Care Daily for October 24, 2026.
Today we will review 3 recent ICU-relevant publications.
The format is quick listen first, then PICO, key results, critical appraisal, bedside impact, and medical English notes.
Use this as a morning triage tool, then open the source link for full-text appraisal before changing practice.

Among 2760 patients, strong stop advice occurred earlier in those allocated to the procalcitonin-guided group compared with the C-reactive protein-guided group (mean difference -1.7 days, 95%CI -2.5 to -0.9, p < 0.001).
C-reactive protein guidance generated a higher proportion of standard care advice (mean difference -9.1%, 95%CI -10.9% to -7.3%, p < 0.001).

Overall advice adherence was greater in patients allocated to the C-reactive protein group than those allocated to the procalcitonin group (mean difference -6.8%, 95%CI -9.0 to -4.5, p < 0.001), driven by the higher proportion of standard care advice and later stronger stop advice with higher adherence (mean difference -14.3%, 95%CI -21.8 to -6.8, p < 0.001).
For critical appraisal, focus on whether the design supports a causal conclusion and whether the patients resemble your ICU population.
The bedside implication is this: This may refine antibiotic selection in selected infected patients, but it should be integrated with local microbiology, renal risk, stewardship, and source control.
Useful English phrase: these findings should be interpreted cautiously because the details of design and applicability matter.

The cohort included 16 599 newborns born at 35 weeks' gestation or later who underwent early POS at 2 to 6 hours of age (8349 [50.3%] female; mean [SD] gestational age, 39.8 [1.3] weeks).
POS results were negative in 16 160 newborns (97.4%), recovered in 208 (1.3%), and positive in 231 (1.4%).

Compared with a negative POS result, a recovered or positive POS result was associated with higher risk of NICU admission (adjusted risk ratio [ARR], 5.62 [95% CI, 4.58-6.91] and 13.04 [95% CI, 11.77-14.44], respectively) and continued hospitalization at 7 days (ARR, 4.70 [95% CI, 3.07-7.19] and 11.97 [95% CI, 9.26-15.47], respectively).
For critical appraisal, focus on whether the design supports a causal conclusion and whether the patients resemble your ICU population.
The bedside implication is this: For most ICU patients, this supports avoiding very tight glucose targets unless a protocol can reliably prevent severe hypoglycemia.
Useful English phrase: these findings should be interpreted cautiously because the details of design and applicability matter.

script.heading: Outro
sentences: That wraps up today's journal club style update.
Before applying any finding, check the full source, the absolute effect size, and your local ICU context.
For English practice, repeat one academic phrase from each article out loud.

articles.title: Delivery and adherence of biomarker-guided antibiotic treatment protocols in the ADAPT-Sepsis clinical trial: an in-trial descriptive process evaluation of daily procalcitonin- and C-reactive protein-guided protocols.
articles.summary: Biomarker-guided antibiotic protocols using daily procalcitonin or C-reactive protein have been proposed to optimise antibiotic duration in sepsis. Patients were assigned to procalcitonin-guided, C-reactive protein-guided or standard care. Algorithm-generated recommendations (strong stop, suggest stop or standard care) were relayed to research staff and clinicians who remained blinded to group allocation. Among 2760 patients, strong stop advice occurred earlier in those allocated to the procalcitonin-guided group compared with the C-reactive protein-guided group (mean difference -1.7 days, 95%CI -2.5 to -0.9, p < 0.001). C-reactive protein guidance generated a higher proportion of standard care advice (mean difference -9.1%, 95%CI -10.9% to -7.3%, p < 0.001).

articles.summary: This population-based cohort study included asymptomatic neonates born at 35 weeks' gestation or later who underwent early POS at 2 to 6 hours of age at a tertiary-level university hospital in Eastern Finland between January 1, 2012, and December 31, 2019. Positive POS result or indeterminate POS result that normalized to a negative POS result (recovered) with repeat testing. Primary outcomes were neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) admission and continued hospitalization at 7 days; secondary outcomes included diagnostic investigations and neonatal morbidities. The cohort included 16 599 newborns born at 35 weeks' gestation or later who underwent early POS at 2 to 6 hours of age (8349 [50.3%] female; mean [SD] gestational age, 39.8 [1.3] weeks). POS results were negative in 16 160 newborns (97.4%), recovered in 208 (1.3%), and positive in 231 (1.4%).

articles.summary: Cerebral CTA did not confirm cerebral circulatory arrest in 15/118 (13%) patients, yielding an overall sensitivity of 87.3% (95%CI 79.6-92.5%). Notably, 93.3% (95%CI 66.0-99.7%) of false-negative results occurred within 12 h of the onset of initial signs of brainstem areflexia.
